<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Notes receivable which relate to real estate financing arrangements that exceed one year, bear interest at a market rate based on the borrower's credit quality and are recorded at face value. &nbsp;Interest is recognized over the life of the note. &nbsp;We require collateral for the notes.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>A note receivable may be considered impaired pursuant to criteria established in Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No. 114, (SFAS 114), <I>Accounting by Creditors for Impairment of a Loan</I>. &nbsp;Pursuant to SFAS 114, a note is impaired if it is probable that we will not collect all principal and interest contractually due. &nbsp;The impairment is measured based on the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the note's effective interest rate. &nbsp;When ultimate collectability of the principal balance of the impaired note is in doubt, all cash receipts on impaired notes are applied to reduce the principal amount of such notes until the principal has been recovered. &nbsp;All cash receipts recognized thereafter are recorded as interest income. &nbsp;Based on our judgment, no notes receivable were impaired for the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004, of which $448 and $3,176 are included in developments in progress, respectively. &nbsp;See Note 11 Commitments and Contingencies for further discussion regarding the $448 note receivable outstanding at December 31, 2005.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We use derivative instruments (specifically the sale of call options on equity securities we hold) to manage exposures from price, interest rate, and credit risks related to the equity securities held. &nbsp;Our objectives for holding derivatives include reducing, eliminating, and efficiently managing the economic impact of these exposures as effectively as possible. Derivative instruments are recognized as either assets or liabilities and are measured at fair value as they are not designated as hedging instruments under Statements of Financial Accounting Standards 133 (SFAS 133) <I>Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities</I>. &nbsp;Gains and losses from changes in fair values of these derivatives, which are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes, are recognized in earnings.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On December 16, 2004, the FASB issued SFAS No. 123R, (SFAS 123R), <I>Accounting for Stock-Based Compensation</I> as amended. &nbsp;SFAS 123R replaces SFAS No. 123, as amended by SFAS No. 148, which we adopted on January 1, 2003. &nbsp;<BR>
SFAS 123R requires that the compensation cost relating to share-based payment transactions to be recognized in financial statements and be measured based on the fair value of the equity or liability instruments issued. &nbsp;SFAS 123R is effective as of the first annual reporting period that begins after June 15, 2005. &nbsp;The adoption of SFAS 123R is not expected to have a material effect on our consolidated financial statements.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In March 2005, the FASB issued Interpretation No. 47 (FIN 47), <I>Accounting for Conditional Asset Retirement Obligations, an interpretation of FASB Statement No. 143</I>. <FONT COLOR=#00007F>&nbsp;</FONT>FIN 47 refers to a legal obligation to perform an asset retirement activity in which the timing and/or method of settlement are conditional on a future event that may or may not be within the control of the entity. <FONT COLOR=#00007F>&nbsp;</FONT>An entity is required to recognize a liability for the fair value of a conditional asset retirement obligation if the fair value of the liability can be reasonable estimated. The fair value of a liability for the conditional asset retirement obligation should be recognized when incurred, generally upon acquisition, construction, or development and through the normal operation of the asset. <FONT COLOR=#00007F>&nbsp;</FONT>This interpretation is effective no later than the end of fiscal years ending after December 31, 2005. <FONT COLOR=#00007F>&nbsp;The a</FONT>doption <FONT COLOR=#00007F>of FIN 47 </FONT>did not have a material effect on <FONT COLOR=#00007F>our</FONT> consolidated financial statements.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In June 2005 the FASB ratified the consensus by the Emerging Issues Task Force (EITF) regarding EITF 04-05, <I>Determining Whether a General Partner or the General Partners, as a Group, Controls a Limited Partnership or Similar Entity When the Limited Partners have Certain Rights</I>. &nbsp;This consensus established the presumption that general partners in a limited partnership control that limited partnership regardless of the extent of the general partners&#146; ownership interest in the limited partnership. The consensus further establishes that the rights of the limited partners can overcome the presumption of control by the general partners, if the limited partners have either (a) the substantive ability to dissolve (liquidate) the limited partnership or otherwise remove the general partners without cause or (b) substantive participating rights. Whether the presumption of control is overcome is a matter of judgment based on the facts and circumstances, for which the consensus provides additional guidance. This consensus is currently applicable to <FONT COLOR=#00007F>us</FONT> for new or modified partnerships, and will otherwise be applicable to existing partnerships in 2006. This consensus applies to limited </P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Prior to our acquisition of the property management companies and our former advisor on December 29, 2004, we were obligated to pay an advisor asset management fee of not more than 1% of our net asset value to our former advisor. &nbsp;Our net asset value was defined as the total book value of the assets invested in equity interests and loans receivable secured by real estate, before reserves for depreciation, reserves for bad debt or other similar non-cash reserves, reduced by any mortgages payable on the respective assets. &nbsp;We computed our net asset value by taking the average of these values at the end of each month for which we were calculating the fee. &nbsp;The fee was payable quarterly in an amount equal to 1/4 of 1% of net asset value as of the last day of the immediately preceding quarter. &nbsp;For any year in which we qualified as a REIT prior to the completion of the transaction, our former advisor was required to reimburse us for certain amounts to the extent that the annual return to shareholders was less than 7%. &nbsp;No reimbursements from our former advisor were required in any year. &nbsp;For the year December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003, we incurred none, $18,958 and $15,531, respectively, of asset management fees. &nbsp;None remain unpaid as of December 31, 2005 and 2004. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>of December 31, 2005 and 2004, options to acquire 14 and 20 shares of common stock were outstanding, respectively.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In addition to selling commissions, the dealer manager of our offerings, an affiliate of our former advisor, has the right to purchase soliciting dealer warrants which are re-allowed to the soliciting dealer. &nbsp;The holder of a soliciting dealer warrant will be entitled to purchase one share from us at a price of $12.00 per share during the period commencing one year from the date of the first issuance of any of the soliciting dealer warrants and ending five years after the effective date of each offering. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005 and 2004, 8,551 had been issued, of which 547 have expired as of December 31, 2005. &nbsp;As of January 31, 2006, approximately 2,002 warrants have expired. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005, no warrants had been exercised. &nbsp;As of March 3, 2006, 44 warrants have been exercised.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On August 23, 2005, our shareholders approved an Equity Award Plan (EAP) and an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP). &nbsp;The EAP will allow certain of our employees to be awarded stock shares and/or stock options. &nbsp;The purpose of the EAP is to provide an incentive to those employees so that we can retain executive level talent. &nbsp;The EAP will be available only to employees of ours. &nbsp;We have reserved 300 shares of common stock under the EAP with awards to be granted prior to June 2015. &nbsp;Our Board of Directors may amend this plan at any time.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On August 23, 2005, we granted twenty-five thousand stock options to an executive employee at an exercise price of $10.75 per share and a term of ten years. &nbsp;These options vest and become exercisable over three years, in one-third installments, commencing August 23, 2006.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The ESPP will allow our employees to purchase our shares of stock on favorable terms and pay for the purchases through periodic payroll deductions all in accordance with current Internal Revenue Service rules and regulations. &nbsp;The purpose of the ESPP is to provide our employees with an opportunity to have a stake in the success of the company. &nbsp;The ESPP will be available only to employees of ours. &nbsp;We have reserved 200 shares of common stock under the ESPP with these shares available through June 30, 2007. &nbsp;The ESPP became available to our employees on January 1, 2006. &nbsp;The purchase price of the shares will be at 85% of fair market value and be limited to five thousand shares or $25 per employee per calendar year. &nbsp;We will incur, as an expense, the 15% discount. &nbsp;Our Board of Directors may amend this plan at any time.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>5.&nbsp;&nbsp;Leases</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Master Lease Agreements</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:6.4pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In conjunction with certain acquisitions, we receive payments under master lease agreements pertaining to some non-revenue producing spaces at the time of purchase, for periods ranging from one to three years after the date of the purchase or until the spaces are leased. &nbsp;GAAP requires that as these payments are received, they be recorded as a reduction in the purchase price of the respective property rather than as rental income. &nbsp;The cumulative amount of such payments was $22,377 and $18,017 as of December 31, 2005 and 2004, respectively.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt; page-break-before:always" align=center>INLAND RETAIL REAL ESTATE TRUST, INC.<BR>
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements<BR>
(In thousands, except per share amounts)</P>
<P style="margin:0pt"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The majority of the revenues from our properties consists of rents received under long-term operating leases. &nbsp;Some leases provide for the payment of fixed base rent paid monthly in advance, and for the reimbursement by tenants to us for the tenant's pro rata share of certain operating expenses including real estate taxes, special assessments, insurance, utilities, common area maintenance, management fees, and certain building repairs paid by the landlord and recoverable under the terms of the lease. &nbsp;Under these leases, the landlord pays all expenses and is reimbursed by the tenant for the tenant's pro rata share of recoverable expenses paid. &nbsp;Certain other tenants are subject to net leases which provide that the tenant is responsible for fixed based rent as well as all costs and expenses associated with occupancy. &nbsp;Under net leases where all expenses are paid directly by the tenant rather than the landlord, such expenses are not included in the consolidated statements of operations. &nbsp;Under net leases where all expenses are paid by the landlord, subject to reimbursement by the tenant, the expenses are included within property operating expenses and reimbursements are included in tenant recovery income on the consolidated statements of operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>A lease termination by a major tenant could result in lease terminations or reductions in rent by other tenants whose leases permit cancellation or rent reduction if a major tenant's lease is terminated. &nbsp;In certain properties where there are large tenants, other tenants may require that if certain large tenants or &quot;shadow&quot; tenants discontinue operations, a right of termination or reduced rent may exist.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The remaining lease terms range from one year to fifty-four years.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Certain tenant leases contain provisions providing for stepped rent increases and rent abatements. &nbsp;GAAP requires us to record rental income for the period of occupancy using the effective monthly rent, which is the average monthly rent for the entire period of occupancy during the term of the lease. &nbsp;As a direct result of recording the effective monthly rent, the accompanying Consolidated Financial Statements include a net increase in rental income of $11,712, $10,445 and $8,231 for the years ended December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003, respectively. &nbsp;The related accounts and rents receivable, net of allowance, for the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004 were $32,528 and $21,523, respectively. &nbsp;We anticipate collecting these amounts over the terms of the related leases as scheduled rent payments are made.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We believe we can achieve the optimum balance between risk and return to our shareholders by leveraging our properties at approximately 50% to 60% of their value. &nbsp;We also believe that we can borrow at the lowest overall cost of funds by placing individual financing on each of the properties. &nbsp;Accordingly, mortgage loans have generally been placed on each property at the time that the property is purchased, or shortly thereafter, with the property securing the financing.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>For the year ended December 31, 2005 and 2004, we closed on or assumed mortgage debt with a principal amount of $48,939 and $269,284, net of mortgage debt repaid. &nbsp;The average costs of funds at December 31, 2005 and 2004 were approximately 5.05% and 5.03%, respectively.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Individual decisions regarding interest rates, loan-to-value, fixed versus variable rate financing, maturity dates and related matters are often based on the condition of the financial markets at the time the debt is placed. &nbsp;Although the loans placed by us are generally non-recourse, occasionally, when it is deemed to be advantageous, we may guarantee all or a portion of the debt. &nbsp;At times, we have borrowed funds as part of a cross-collateralized package, with cross-default provisions, in order to enhance the benefits of the financing. &nbsp;In those circumstances, one or more of the properties may secure the debt of another of our properties.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:11pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The fair value of mortgages payable is the amount at which the instrument could be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties. &nbsp;The fair value of our mortgages is estimated to be approximately $2,323,000 at December 31, 2005. &nbsp;We estimate the fair value of our mortgages payable by discounting the future cash flows of each instrument at rates currently offered to us for similar debt instruments of comparable maturities by our lenders. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The principal balance of $239,210 or 10.4% of our mortgages payable at December 31, 2005, have variable interest rates averaging 4.36%. &nbsp;An increase in the variable interest rate on certain mortgages payable constitutes a market risk.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The majority of our loans require monthly payments of interest only, although some loans require principal and interest payments, as well as reserves for taxes, insurance, and certain other costs. &nbsp;Interest on variable rate loans are currently based on LIBOR (London Inter-Bank Offering Rate which is a financial industry standard benchmark rate), plus a spread ranging from 132 to 185 basis points. &nbsp;Variable rate loans may be prepaid without penalty, while fixed-rate loans generally may be prepaid with a penalty, after specific lockout periods.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We paid off or refinanced all of the debt that matured during 2005 and 2004. &nbsp;In those cases where maturing debt was repaid from new financing obtained, the replacement financing was for amounts which differ from the loans retired, either producing or requiring cash on a property by property basis. &nbsp;We intend to pay off or refinance all debt that matures in 2006.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On May 7, 2005, we renewed the line of credit with three financial institutions in the amount of $100,000 of which none was outstanding at December 31, 2005. &nbsp;This line of credit has an accordion feature which will allow us to increase the line of credit up to $250,000 if the need arises. &nbsp;The line of credit is available to us for one year with an option to renew annually for two consecutive years. &nbsp;We expect to renew this facility in 2006. &nbsp;This facility requires that we comply with certain financial covenants, which include a limitation on the ratio of our debt to the value of our total assets, based on a specific formula, as well as the level of our earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) as compared to overall interest expense. &nbsp;We were in compliance with those covenants for the reporting period ending December 31, 2005. &nbsp;This line of credit gives us flexibility in fulfilling our acquisition strategy, funding our development activities and maintaining overall liquidity to meet operating requirements. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>7.&nbsp;&nbsp;Investment in Unconsolidated Joint Venture</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Inland-SAU Retail Fund, L.L.C. (SAU JV) was formed on May 13, 2005. &nbsp;SAU JV is a strategic joint venture formed between us and Special Account-U, L.P. (SAU), an affiliate of Henderson Global Investors (North America) Inc., an advisor to an institutional investor. &nbsp;Under the joint venture agreement, SAU will contribute 80% of the equity capital (up to $100,000) and we will contribute 20% of the equity capital (up to $25,000) required to acquire retail properties located east of the Mississippi that satisfy certain investment guidelines, as defined, unless waived by SAU JV. As of December 31, 2005, we had contributed approximately $15,300. &nbsp;SAU and us may increase our equity capital commitments by an additional $25,000 and $6,250, respectively, in accordance with the terms of the joint venture agreement. &nbsp;Funds contributed to SAU JV will be used primarily to acquire properties located in our target markets that satisfy certain parameters (unless waived by the parties), in addition to our current acquisition underwriting guidelines. &nbsp;The SAU JV owns 21 properties as of December 31, 2005. &nbsp;During the year ended December 31, 2005, we initially acquired twelve properties and subsequently sold them at our cost to the SAU JV upon completion of due diligence by SAU. &nbsp;The results of operations of these properties prior to the sale to the SAU JV have not been recorded by us as discontinued operations due to our continuing involvement with the properties. &nbsp; &nbsp;
</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Cash flow from the operations of the retail properties is to be distributed monthly to SAU and us according to our percentage interests, currently 80% and 20%, respectively. For the period May 13, 2005 to December 31, 2005, we received approximately $140 in distributions of cash flow from operations.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Cash flow from a major capital event, as defined, is to be distributed in the following order:</P>
<P style="line-height:10pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-10pt; padding-left:72pt; text-indent:-18pt; font-family:Symbol; font-size:8pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.15pt; padding-left:72pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">First, in an amount equal to the unreturned capital of SAU and us; and</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:10pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-10pt; padding-left:72pt; text-indent:-18pt; font-family:Symbol; font-size:8pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.15pt; padding-left:72pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Second, if the internal rate of return to SAU and us, as defined, is less than 11%, according to the percentage interests of SAU and us; and</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:10pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-10pt; padding-left:72pt; text-indent:-18pt; font-family:Symbol; font-size:8pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.15pt; padding-left:72pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Third, if the internal rate of return to SAU and us is between 11% and 13%, a 5% incentive distribution, as defined, to us and the balance according to the percentage interests of SAU and us; and</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:10pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-10pt; padding-left:72pt; text-indent:-18pt; font-family:Symbol; font-size:8pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.15pt; padding-left:72pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Fourth, if the internal rate of return to SAU and us is greater than 13%, a 25% incentive distribution to us and the balance according to the percentage interests of SAU and us.</FONT></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>SAU JV&#146;s profit and loss for each year is to be allocated to SAU and us in amounts necessary to cause their respective capital accounts to reflect the distribution of cash flow from a hypothetical liquidation of SAU JV&#146;s assets and liabilities. Our portion of SAU JV&#146;s net loss was $9 for the period May 13, 2005 to December 31, 2005 which is a component of other income in the accompanying Consolidated Statement of Operations. However, in any year we are paid an incentive distribution, we will receive a special allocation in an amount equal to such incentive distribution. &nbsp;Any special allocations to us will reduce profit or increase the loss to be allocated to SAU and us.</P>
<P style="margin:0pt" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>SAU JV intends to obtain non-recourse debt financing from our joint venture partner or other institutional lenders in an amount no greater than 60% of the total cost of each acquired property. &nbsp;SAU JV anticipates that such debt financings will be interest only, having fixed or variable rates with scheduled maturities of five to seven years. &nbsp;In order to expedite the acquisition of a retail property, either SAU or us may advance funds to SAU JV until debt financing is obtained. &nbsp;Such advances will be evidenced by a note due on demand, bearing a market rate of interest and secured by the respective retail property. For the period May 13, 2005 to December 31, 2005, we funded approximately $78,250 of advances to SAU and as part of the first four acquisitions, we provided approximately $41,000 in interim financing on these properties. As of December 31, 2005 the advances and interim financing had been repaid.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The acquisition fees we earned relative to the properties acquired by the SAU JV are recorded in other income, net of the fees related to our 20% equity contribution to the SAU JV, totaling approximately $846 for the year ended December 31, 2005. &nbsp;The SAU JV plans to acquire additional properties using leverage consistent with its existing business plan to achieve its investment objectives.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The SAU JV agreement also allows for either of the SAU JV partners to offer to acquire the other partner&#146;s interests in the SAU JV after the second anniversary date of the agreement. &nbsp;In the event of an acquisition of the other partner&#146;s interest in the SAU JV, there may be termination costs related to the early payoff of existing financing. &nbsp;SAU and we have agreed that in connection with any change of control, the party that acquired the other partner&#146;s interest in the SAU JV shall be responsible for and have the benefit of any financial impact related to the repayment of the existing financing. &nbsp;The SAU JV agreement also allows us to exercise an option, anytime prior to the second anniversary date of the agreement, to offer to buy out SAU&#146;s interest if the SAU JV is unable to reach unanimous agreement as to any major decisions, including decisions regarding acquisition of properties by the SAU JV. &nbsp;All major decisions require the approval of both SAU JV partners and as such we account for our investment using the equity method of accounting.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In addition to the SAU JV agreement, we also entered into a contract with a financial advisor to provide capital raising services related to this SAU JV. &nbsp;We will pay them a fee equal to 2% of the capital contributed by SAU. &nbsp;This fee is earned pro-rata over the five year period commencing one year from the date of each contribution, and is partially refundable to us if one of the SAU JV partners sells its ownership interest to the other at any point during that time. &nbsp;These fees are capitalized as part of our investment in this unconsolidated joint venture. &nbsp;Such fees totaled approximately $1,151 for the year ended December 31, 2005. &nbsp;Of these fees, $981 remain unpaid as of December 31, 2005.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We, through our property management companies, provide management and leasing services to the SAU JV for a monthly property management and leasing fee of 4.5% of actual gross income on the properties, payable monthly, in arrears. &nbsp;We earned fees of approximately $135 for the year ended December 31, 2005.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>8.&nbsp;&nbsp;Recent Developments</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On January 11, 2005, we entered into a lease termination agreement with a tenant relating to approximately 49,000 square feet of space at our property known as Valley Park Commons, located in Hagerstown, Maryland, in exchange for a lease termination payment of $1,850. &nbsp;The lease termination was received August 18, 2005 and is included in rental income. &nbsp;In connection with this lease termination, we recorded lease termination fee income of $1,687 for the year ended December 31, 2005, which represents the termination payment described above, less related outstanding receivables, including deferred rent receivables.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In 2005, we received approximately three thousand shares of Sears Holding stock as an additional termination fee on the leases for three Kmart stores at three of our properties located in Plant City, Florida, Bradenton, Florida and Macon, Georgia. &nbsp;We recorded termination fee income of approximately $385 for the year ended December 31, 2005, which represents the value of the stock described above and is included in rental income.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We acquired nine retail properties and four land parcels for future development totaling approximately 462,000 square feet and 44 acres, respectively. &nbsp;We acquired 12 properties totaling approximately 808,000 square feet on behalf of SAU JV. &nbsp;These properties were subsequently sold to SAU JV upon completion of the due diligence process by SAU. &nbsp;We also funded 11 earnouts at five of our existing properties totaling approximately 77,000 square feet. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We sold one office building totaling approximately 4,700 square feet and three outlots totaling approximately four acres for an aggregate sales price of $2,620. &nbsp;As a result of these dispositions and properties sold to SAU JV, we have recognized gains of $2,515.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During 2005, we closed on 15 mortgages payable, including eight mortgages payable subsequently assumed by SAU JV when they acquired the related properties from us, resulting in net proceeds of $51,316. &nbsp;These mortgages payable have fixed interest rates ranging from 4.60% to 5.50%. &nbsp;We refinanced two mortgages payable that matured in 2005 resulting in additional proceeds of $575, net of the debt repaid. &nbsp;The new mortgages payable have fixed interest rates of 4.57% and 4.73%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>9.&nbsp;&nbsp;Segment Reporting</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We own and seek to acquire multi-tenant shopping centers in the eastern United States. &nbsp;All of our shopping centers are currently located in Georgia, Florida, North Carolina, South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Alabama, Tennessee, Ohio, New Jersey, Maryland, Texas, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Illinois, New York, Rhode Island, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Colorado, Michigan, Washington, California, Louisiana and Oklahoma. &nbsp;Our shopping centers are typically anchored by grocery and drug stores or other national/regional tenants and are complemented with additional stores providing a wide range of other goods and services to shoppers.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We assess and measure operating results on an individual property basis for each of our properties based on net property operations. &nbsp;Since all of our properties exhibit highly similar economic characteristics, cater to the day-to-day living needs of their respective surrounding communities, and offer similar degrees of risk and opportunities for growth, the properties have been aggregated and reported as one operating segment.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>10.&nbsp;&nbsp;Earnings (Loss) per Share</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Basic earnings (loss) per share (EPS) is computed by dividing net income (loss) by the basic weighted average number of common shares outstanding for the period (the common shares). &nbsp;Diluted EPS is computed by dividing net income by the common shares plus shares issuable upon exercise of existing options or other contracts calculated under the treasury method. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003, options to purchase 22, 20 and 15 shares of common stock, respectively, at an exercise price of $9.05 per share were outstanding. &nbsp;These options were not included in the computation of basic or diluted EPS as the effect would be immaterial. &nbsp;Under the merger agreement, 19,700 shares were held in escrow and a portion was released on the first anniversary of the merger closing date and the balance is to be released on the 540<SUP>th</SUP> day after the merger closing date, subject in both cases to any pending claims of ours for indemnification under the merger agreement. &nbsp;The shares held in escrow are included in the basic and diluted weighted average number of common shares.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As of December 31, 2005 and 2004, warrants to purchase 8,004 and 8,004 shares of common stock at a price of $12.00 per share were outstanding, respectively. &nbsp;These warrants were not included in the computation of diluted EPS because the exercise price of such warrants was greater than the average market price of common shares. &nbsp;As of March 3, 2006, 44 warrants had been exercised.</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>11.&nbsp;&nbsp;Commitments and Contingencies</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We are at various stages in the development and redevelopment of eleven projects. &nbsp;Certain of our development projects are structured in conjunction with other developers. &nbsp;When we engage in these projects, we concurrently enter into a co-development agreement with an unrelated developer to oversee the project, including supervision of the general contractor and leasing activities. &nbsp;We only enter into these types of projects when at least one anchor tenant's lease is signed, at which time we acquire the land. &nbsp;Under the co-development agreement, the developer is entitled to a base fee generally paid monthly and an incentive fee calculated on the operating cash flow of the project upon completion. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>For those projects which we solely develop, we generally attempt to place as many tenants as possible under lease before we acquire the land. &nbsp;This reduces the risk associated with development. &nbsp;However, in certain circumstances, particularly if we believe land can be purchased at a favorable price, we may close on the land and develop the property at a later date. &nbsp;Prior to closing on any property we confirm that appropriate zoning exists, that utilities are or will be available to the site and that soil conditions allow for the construction of our intended development.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Several properties we have purchased have earnout components, meaning that we did not pay for portions of these properties that were not rent producing. &nbsp;We are obligated, under certain agreements, to pay a higher purchase price when such vacant space is rented, a tenant moves into its space and begins to pay rent. &nbsp;The earnout payments are based on a pre-determined formula applied to the rental rates achieved. &nbsp;Each earnout agreement has a time limit regarding the obligation to pay any additional monies. &nbsp;If at the end of the time period allowed, certain space has not been leased and occupied, we will own that space without any additional obligation. &nbsp;Based on pro forma leasing rates, we may pay as much as $18,391 in the future, as retail space covered by earnout agreements is occupied and becomes rent producing.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We periodically agree to fund construction costs related to the build-out of tenant spaces covered by earnout agreements at certain of our shopping centers. &nbsp;Each note receivable related to such funding requires monthly interest payments with the entire principal due at the earlier of maturity or at the time we make our earnout payment. &nbsp;Interest received on these notes is applied as a reduction to our final cost of the rental space covered by an earnout agreement.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>At December 31, 2005 and 2004, notes receivable totaled $448 and $3,176, respectively, and is included in developments in progress on our accompanying Consolidated Balance Sheets.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On February 20, 2006, we reached an agreement with the developer of one of our properties to forgive a $448 note receivable which matured on December 31, 2005. &nbsp;We funded the $448 as part of a construction loan with the developer who built 12,000 square feet of retail space but was unable to secure a tenant for the space as required under the terms of an earnout agreement. &nbsp;We determined that it was advantageous for us to receive a deed to the retail space and forgive the note because, in our judgment, it would have cost significantly more than $448 if we were to construct the property ourselves. &nbsp;The developer also agreed to pay interest on the loan owed through the date of the agreement.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On January 4, 2006, a citizens&#146; suit was brought against 18 parties, including government officials, under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act to clean up 12 sites in Jersey City, New Jersey on which chromium-bearing waste was generated by prior owners of those sites or on sites adjacent to those sites. &nbsp;The defendants include Inland Southeast Jersey City, L.L.C. (&#147;Inland Southeast&#146;), a wholly-owned subsidiary of a limited partnership subsidiary of ours, which owns one of the sites, known as 440 Commons (the &#147;Property&#148;), a retail shopping center containing approximately 162,000 leasable square feet, built in 1997 and acquired by Inland Southeast in 2003. &nbsp;The entire Property contains a geothermal lining under an asphalt cap designed to prevent the soil contamination from coming into contact with users of the Property. &nbsp;The Property is subject to a No Further Action letter from the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection with respect to soil contamination. &nbsp;The complaint alleges, among other things, that contaminated groundwater has reached the </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="line-height:10pt; margin:0pt; font-size:8pt" align=center>82</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; padding-bottom:3pt; border-bottom:3pt solid #DFDFDF"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt; page-break-before:always" align=center>INLAND RETAIL REAL ESTATE TRUST, INC.<BR>
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements<BR>
(In thousands, except per share amounts)</P>

<P style="margin:0pt"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Hackensack River and requests that Inland Southeast remove and dispose of the contamination in the soil and groundwater on the site, and requests attorneys fees and costs, and such other relief as the Court deems appropriate.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We intend to vigorously defend this action, and believe we have meritorious defenses to contest the claims asserted by the plaintiffs. &nbsp;Based upon available information, we are not able to determine the financial impact, if any, of such action, but we believe that the outcome will not have a material adverse effect on our consolidated financial position or results of operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>12.&nbsp;&nbsp;Provision for Asset Impairment</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During the fourth quarter of 2005, we recorded an asset impairment of $5,800 related to an approximately 102,000 square foot, single-user retail property located in Macon, Georgia. &nbsp;The former tenant, Kmart, filed for bankruptcy in 2003, rejected the lease and vacated the property. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005 we determined that the carrying value of the property exceeded the fair value using present value techniques and therefore an impairment loss was recorded.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During the fourth quarter of 2004, we recorded an asset impairment of $2,056 related to an approximately 17,000 square foot, single-user property located in Augusta, Georgia. &nbsp;The former tenant, Just for Feet, filed for bankruptcy in 2004, rejected the lease and vacated the property. &nbsp;During the fourth quarter 2004, and after our diligent efforts to re-tenant the property, we decided that redeveloping the property was the most appropriate choice to enhance shareholder value. &nbsp;Construction was complete as of December 31, 2005 and we expect the property to be placed in service in 2006.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>13.&nbsp;&nbsp;Derivative Instruments</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>For the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004, we sold call options on equity securities we held. &nbsp;For the year ended December 31, 2003, derivative instruments were not utilized. &nbsp;For the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004, no derivative instruments were designated as hedges as determined in accordance with SFAS 133. &nbsp;Gains and losses from changes in fair values of derivatives that are not designated as a hedge for accounting purposes did not have a significant impact on earnings for the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004. &nbsp;A loss of $6 for the year ended December 31, 2004 from changes in fair values of derivatives were recognized in earnings as part of other income. &nbsp;A gain of $91 for the year ended December 31, 2004, upon the expiration of derivatives that are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes, was recognized in earnings as part of other income.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:8.25pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>14.&nbsp;&nbsp;Subsequent Events</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On January 18, 2006, we increased the price to sell or buy our shares under the DRP and the SRP, effective February 7, 2006, to $10.50.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We paid distributions of $18,007, $17,917 and $17,960 to our shareholders in January, February and March 2006, respectively.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Through the DRP and SRP, we issued a net of 1,228 shares of common stock from January 1, 2006 through March 3, 2006, resulting in a total of 259,452 shares of common stock outstanding.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>From the period beginning January 1, 2006 through March 3, 2006 we have purchased two properties and one land parcel comprising approximately 28,000 square feet and 12 acres, respectively, for approximately $14,203. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As of January 31 2006, approximately 2,002 warrants have expired. &nbsp;From the period beginning January 1, 2006 to March 3, 2006, 44 warrants have been exercised.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We closed on two mortgages payable totaling $5,441 and repaid one mortgage payable totaling $3,600, subsequent to December 31, 2005. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<B>Item 9(A).&nbsp;&nbsp; Controls and Procedures<A NAME="_Toc116275210"></A><A NAME="_Toc129568145"></A><A NAME="_Toc129593428"></A></B></P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<B>Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures</B>. &nbsp;We have established disclosure controls and procedures to ensure that material information relating to the company, including its consolidated subsidiaries, is made known to the officers who certify our financial reports and to the members of our senior management and the Board of Directors.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
Based on management's evaluation as of December 31 2005, our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer have concluded that our disclosure controls and procedures (as defined in Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934) are effective to ensure that the information required to be disclosed by us in our reports that we file or submit under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the Securities and Exchange Commission's rules and forms.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<B>Management's Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting</B>. &nbsp;Our management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting, as such term is defined in Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(f). &nbsp;Under the supervision and with the participation of our management, including our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, we conducted an evaluation of the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting based on the framework <I>Internal Control &#150; Integrated Framework</I> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. &nbsp;Based on our evaluation under the framework in <I>Internal Control &#150; Integrated Framework</I>, our management concluded that our internal control over financial reporting was effective as of December 31, 2005. &nbsp;Management's assessment of the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 has been audited by KPMG LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, as stated in their report which is included herein.</P>
<P style="line-height:13pt; margin:0pt; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<B>Changes in Internal Control</B>. &nbsp;There were no changes to our internal controls over financial reporting during the fourth quarter ended December 31, 2005 that has materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, our internal controls over financial reporting.</P>
